note.question: How should estimation and experimental design be coordinated?
note.overview: Switchback experiments, in which experimental units are assigned to control and treatment interchangeably over time, have gained increasing popularity in recent years due to their ability to mitigate interference across units. Despite their wide adoption in the technology sector, drawing reliable inferences from such experiments remains challenging due to temporal interference. In this paper, we address this challenge by examining a special causal structure commonly found in a wide range of applications.

source.quote: Switchback experiments, in which experimental units are assigned to control and treatment interchangeably over time, have gained increasing popularity in recent years due to their ability to mitigate interference across units.
For example, con­ sider a ride-hailing platform testing a new customer fare policy in a city.
For example, con­ sider a ride-hailing platform testing a new customer fare policy in a city.

Traditional A/B testing, which ran­ domly assigns half of the city districts to the old fare (control group) and the other half to the new fare (treat­ ment group), would fail to provide an unbiased esti­ mate of the treatment effect.

This is because customers in both groups interact with the same pool of drivers, allowing the group with the fare advantage to monopo­ lize the available supply, thereby introducing bias into the results.
